mcqs.question: Why does an XSS payload effectively bypass the same-origin policy?
options: Because the same-origin policy only applies to requests, not to scripts
Because the injected script is served by, and therefore executes as, the victim site's own origin
Because modern browsers relax the policy for scripts that were user-generated
Because the attacker's domain is added to the page's allowed origin list
mcqs.explanation: The browser has no way to distinguish attacker-supplied markup that arrived inside your page from markup your template authored, so the injected code inherits your origin and all its privileges. Nothing about the policy is relaxed or reconfigured — the policy works exactly as designed, it just cannot tell whose code it is running.

mcqs.question: A researcher reports a working XSS, but your server access logs and WAF show no trace of the payload. Which variety is this most likely to be?
options: DOM-based, with the payload delivered in the URL fragment after the #
Stored, because the payload was written to the database before logging began
Reflected, because reflected payloads are echoed back rather than recorded
None — if it were real, the request would necessarily appear in the logs
mcqs.explanation: Browsers strip everything after the # before sending the request, so a fragment-delivered payload reaches client JavaScript without ever touching the server, its logs, or a WAF. Reflected XSS is the opposite case — the payload rides in the query string or body, so it is very much present in the request the server logs.

mcqs.question: Replacing `element.innerHTML = userText` with `element.textContent = userText` fixes the injection. Why?
options: textContent strips any tags it finds out of the string before inserting it
textContent runs the browser's built-in HTML sanitizer over the value
textContent silently rejects values containing angle brackets
textContent inserts the value as characters and never invokes the HTML parser
mcqs.explanation: textContent sets a text node, so the browser never parses the string as markup and a less-than sign is simply displayed on screen. It is not filtering, stripping, or rejecting anything — the value is preserved intact, which is why it is both safe and lossless.

mcqs.question: Your session cookie is HttpOnly and Secure. An XSS is found on an authenticated page. What can the injected script still do?
options: Nothing meaningful — with the cookie unreadable the session is out of reach
Call your API as the victim, since the browser attaches the cookie to those requests automatically
Only read data already rendered on the current screen, never write anything
Only act after the user re-authenticates, because HttpOnly invalidates the session on injection
mcqs.explanation: HttpOnly blocks document.cookie from reading the token, closing exfiltration — but the browser still attaches that cookie to same-origin requests, so the script can issue state-changing calls and read their responses as the victim. HttpOnly is a meaningful reduction in blast radius, not a mitigation that makes XSS harmless.

mcqs.question: In DOM-based XSS terminology, which pairing correctly describes `location.hash` and `innerHTML`?
options: location.hash is the source and innerHTML is the sink
location.hash is the sink and innerHTML is the source
Both are sources; the sink is whichever DOM node receives the value
Both are sinks; the source is the attacker's crafted link
mcqs.explanation: A source is where attacker-influenceable data enters client code, and a sink is the API that interprets it as markup or code — so the fragment is the source and the markup-parsing assignment is the sink. Calling the crafted link the source confuses delivery with the API surface the vulnerability is actually named for.

mcqs.question: A static marketing site with no database renders visitor User-Agent strings into an internal traffic dashboard. Is stored XSS possible?
options: No — with no database there is nowhere for a payload to be stored
No — the User-Agent header is set by the browser and cannot be controlled by an attacker
Yes — the request log is the store, and the dashboard viewer is the victim
Yes, but only if the marketing site itself renders the header back to visitors
mcqs.explanation: Stored XSS only requires that the payload persist somewhere between the attacker's visit and the victim's, and a log file qualifies exactly as a database row would — with the added problem that the victim is a privileged internal user. Headers are fully attacker-controlled: anything sending an HTTP request chooses its own User-Agent.
